lessons.title: Ask Jo: advice for teens
lessons.description: Two readers write to an advice blog, and Jo answers with what she would do in their place.

material.body:
Dear Jo,
My best friend always copies my homework. At first I didn't mind, but now she asks every single day, and last week our teacher noticed that our answers were the same. I don't want to lose her as a friend. What should I do?
Nina, 15

Dear Nina,
If I were you, I would talk to her before the next test. Be honest but kind: tell her that you're worried about getting into trouble. If she really is a good friend, she'll understand. You could also offer to study together — if you explained the hard parts to her, she wouldn't need to copy. And if the teacher asks you about it, tell the truth.

Dear Jo,
I spend about eight hours a day on my phone. I know it's too much, but whenever I try to stop, I feel bored and I go straight back to it. My marks are getting worse.
Dan, 16

Dear Dan,
You're not alone — lots of people feel the same. If I were in your position, I wouldn't try to stop completely. Start small: turn off notifications after nine and charge your phone outside your bedroom. If you had a hobby that kept your hands busy, like drawing or skateboarding, you would reach for your phone less often. Try it for two weeks and see what happens.

lessons.title: From bean to bar: how chocolate is made
lessons.description: A short article about the journey of chocolate, from the cacao tree to the shop.

material.body:
Chocolate is loved all over the world, but few people know how much work goes into a single bar.

It all starts with the cacao tree, which is grown in hot, wet countries near the equator. Most of the world's cacao is produced in West Africa, especially in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. The fruit, called pods, are cut from the trees by hand, because the trees are too delicate for machines.

Inside each pod there are around forty beans. The beans are taken out, covered with banana leaves and left for about a week. During this time they change colour and start to develop their famous taste. Then they are dried in the sun and sent to factories in other countries.

In the factory, the beans are roasted, and their shells are removed. What is left is crushed into a thick, dark paste. To make milk chocolate, sugar and milk are added. The mixture is stirred for hours until it becomes smooth, and then it is poured into moulds and cooled.

Chocolate was first drunk, not eaten. The Maya and the Aztecs made a bitter drink from cacao more than two thousand years ago. Solid chocolate bars were only invented in the nineteenth century.

lessons.title: Podcast: learning to skate at 19
lessons.description: Lena talks about starting a new hobby later than everyone else.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Welcome to New Hobbies. My guest today is Lena, who started skateboarding at nineteen. Lena, why did you decide to try it?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: I'd always wanted to learn, but I was too scared of falling. Then last year I watched a video of a seventy-year-old woman skating, and I thought: if she can do it, so can I.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: How did the first lesson go?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Honestly, I hated it. I kept falling, and I couldn't stop thinking about the kids watching me. But my teacher told me to keep trying, and by the third lesson I could ride without holding her hand.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: What do you enjoy most about it now?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: I enjoy learning something completely new. At work I'm good at most things, so it's nice to be a beginner again. And I love meeting people at the skatepark — I've made some great friends there.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Any advice for listeners who want to start?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Don't avoid trying just because you're older than everyone else. Buy good protection, find a teacher, and practise a little every day. And remember to have fun!

lessons.title: Dialogue: the missing painting
lessons.description: Two students try to work out what happened to a painting that disappeared from the school hall.

segments.speaker: Ella
segments.text: Have you seen the hall? The big painting of the sea isn't there any more. Someone must have taken it last night.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Last night? It can't have been last night — the school was locked at six, and the alarm didn't go off.

segments.speaker: Ella
segments.text: Then it must have happened this morning. Look, there's a ladder by the wall, and the floor is still wet.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Wet? It might have been the cleaner. They usually wash the floor early.

segments.speaker: Ella
segments.text: But why would a cleaner take a painting? That doesn't make sense. Wait — there's a note on the wall. It says, “Back soon. Mr K.”

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Mr K… that must be Mr Kowalski, the art teacher. He could have taken it to his room to repair the frame. It was broken at the corner, remember?

segments.speaker: Ella
segments.text: You might be right. Or he may have sent it to be cleaned before the parents' evening. Either way, it can't have been stolen. Thieves don't usually leave notes!

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: True. Let's ask him at break before we start a rumour.

segments.speaker: Ella
segments.text: Look, there he is, by the stairs. Mr Kowalski! Did you take the painting from the hall?

segments.speaker: Mr Kowalski
segments.text: I did, yes. I came in at seven this morning to fix the frame before it fell off the wall. Didn’t you see my note?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: We did. Ella was sure that someone must have stolen it in the middle of the night.

segments.speaker: Mr Kowalski
segments.text: Well, she can’t have looked very carefully at the ladder — it’s mine. The painting will be back on the wall by Friday, good as new.

lessons.title: The bridge that was printed
lessons.description: A news article about a steel bridge made by robots with a 3D printer.

material.body:
A footbridge that was printed by robots has been opened to the public in a European city — and it may change the way bridges are built in the future.

The 12-metre steel bridge, which crosses one of the city's old canals, was produced by four robotic arms over six months. Instead of being made from separate parts, it was built up layer by layer from melted steel, in the same way that small plastic objects are made by home 3D printers.

While the bridge was being printed, thousands of tiny sensors were added to its structure. These sensors are now being used to collect information about the bridge: how much it moves, how it reacts to temperature and how many people cross it every day. The data will be analysed by engineers, who hope to learn how 3D-printed metal behaves over many years.

Before it was opened, the bridge had been tested with heavy weights for several weeks to make sure it was safe. According to the designers, it is just as strong as a traditional bridge, but it uses less material and can be produced in shapes that would be impossible with traditional methods.

Critics say the technology is still too slow and expensive to be used for large projects. However, supporters believe that within twenty years many smaller structures, from bus stops to playgrounds, will be printed rather than built.

lessons.title: Things I wish I'd known at fifteen
lessons.description: A blog post in which a 24-year-old looks back at her teenage years.

material.body:
Last week I found my old diary from when I was fifteen. Reading it was funny and a little painful, so I decided to write the post I wish someone had shown me back then.

First, I wish I hadn't worried so much about what other people thought. I spent hours choosing clothes and deleting photos because I was sure everyone was judging me. In reality, everyone was far too busy worrying about themselves.

Second, I wish I had kept playing the piano. I gave up because practising felt boring, and now, at twenty-four, I'm paying for lessons and starting almost from zero. If only someone had told me that boring practice is how you get good at anything!

Third, I wish I had been kinder to my parents. They weren't perfect, but they were trying. My mum still wishes I would call more often — so I've started calling her every Sunday.

Of course, some things I don't regret at all. I'm glad I joined the drama club, even though I was shy, because that's where I met my best friend. And I'm glad I made mistakes, because they taught me more than any advice.

So, if you're fifteen and reading this: relax, keep practising the things you love, and call your mum.

lessons.title: The night the lights went out
lessons.description: A dramatic travel story about a power cut on a mountain train.

material.body:
Never had I seen a sky so full of stars. It was nearly midnight, and our train was climbing slowly through the mountains when, without any warning, every light on board went out.

At first nobody spoke. Then a child started laughing, and the spell was broken. Not only had the lights gone, but the heating had stopped too, and within minutes we could see our breath. Little did we know that we would be sitting there for the next five hours.

Hardly had the conductor walked through the carriage when people began to ask questions. Was there an accident? Would another train come? He shrugged and smiled. “Only when the line is checked,” he said, “will we be able to move.”

Strangely, those five hours turned out to be the best part of the whole trip. Strangers shared blankets, biscuits and stories. An old man taught three teenagers a card game from his childhood; a woman from Brazil sang quietly in Portuguese. Rarely do people talk to each other like that on a normal journey.

No sooner had the lights come back on than everyone returned to their phones, as if nothing had happened. But I still have the address of the old man, and every December he sends me a card with a drawing of a train under the stars.

lessons.title: Interview: a video game sound designer
lessons.description: Maya explains what her job really involves — and what people get wrong about it.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Maya, you design sound for video games. What do people usually get wrong about your job?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: What most people imagine is someone composing music all day. In fact, it's the small sounds that take up most of my time: footsteps, doors, wind, the click of a menu.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Where do those sounds come from?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: Very often, from my kitchen. It was a bag of frozen peas that gave us the sound of a character walking on snow in our last game. All I did was squeeze it slowly next to a microphone.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: That's brilliant. What's the hardest part?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: The thing that's hardest is knowing when to stop. You can always add another layer, another detail. But what players actually notice is when something sounds wrong, not when it sounds perfect.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: How did you get into the industry?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: It was a school project that started it. We had to make a short film, and nobody wanted to do the sound, so I volunteered. What surprised me was how much the sound changed the mood of the whole film. After that, all I wanted to do was record things.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: And what do you love most about the job?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: It's the moment when someone plays the game for the first time and jumps out of their chair. That's when I know the sound is doing its job.

lessons.title: A proposal to the city council
lessons.description: A formal letter from a youth group asking the council to keep the city library open later.

material.body:
Dear Members of the City Council,

We are writing on behalf of the Riverside Youth Forum to propose a change to the opening hours of the Central Library, which currently closes at six o'clock on weekdays.

For many young people in our area, the library is the only quiet place where they can study. A survey we carried out among 300 students found that almost two thirds of them do not have a desk at home, and that most are unable to visit the library before five because of school and part-time jobs. It is therefore essential that the library remain open until at least nine o'clock from Monday to Thursday.

We recognise that longer hours would involve additional costs. We would therefore suggest that the council consider a pilot scheme of six months, during which the number of visitors be recorded each evening. Should the scheme prove unsuccessful, the original hours could be restored. We also propose that volunteers from the Forum be trained to support library staff in the evenings, which would reduce the cost considerably.

A similar scheme in a neighbouring city offers an encouraging example. There, evening opening was introduced two years ago, and the number of young visitors after six o’clock has since tripled. Teachers have also reported that students who use the library in the evenings tend to hand in their homework more regularly. We would be glad to share the details of that scheme with the council.

It is our firm belief that access to a safe place to learn should not depend on one's family circumstances. We respectfully request that this proposal be discussed at the next council meeting, and we would welcome the opportunity to present our survey in person.

Yours faithfully,
The Riverside Youth Forum
